title: SRE for AI — Multi-Agent Incident Response, Runbooks, Predictive Detection

questions.question: What multi-agent shape does the lesson recommend for AI SRE?
options: Random selection of one of three agents, with no supervisor synthesizing their findings
Supervisor agent that breaks the incident into sub-queries for specialized log, metric, and runbook agents, then synthesizes and presents to a human
Two agents in series with no supervisor, each handing off directly to the next without synthesis
One monolithic agent owning everything, from log search to PromQL to runbook retrieval to remediation
questions.explanation: The lesson's architecture is a supervisor that breaks an incident into sub-queries for specialized log, metric, and runbook agents with tool access, which then synthesizes their findings into a hypothesis and presents it to a human for approval.

questions.question: Which auto-remediation set does the lesson call safe?
options: Re-architecting service topology, one of the broad changes the lesson places outside the safe set
Altering databases, one of the broad changes the lesson places outside the safe set
Restart pod, revert a specific deploy, scale a pool within pre-approved bounds, enable a pre-approved feature flag
Modifying IAM policies, one of the broad changes the lesson places outside the safe set
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the line explicitly: restart pod, revert a specific deploy, scale a pool within pre-approved bounds, and enable a pre-approved feature flag are the safe/narrow set; changing topology, IAM, or databases is not safe.

questions.question: How does NeuBird Hawkeye use adversarial evaluation to filter hallucinated root causes?
options: Uses GAN-style training, pitting a generator model against a discriminator during the incident review
Picks the higher-confidence model's answer always, without ever escalating disagreement to a human
Runs the same model twice on the same input, rather than two independent models
Two models independently analyze the same incident; agreement = high confidence, disagreement = escalate to human with both hypotheses
questions.explanation: The lesson describes NeuBird Hawkeye's adversarial evaluation as two models independently analyzing the same incident: agreement signals high confidence, and disagreement escalates to a human with both hypotheses visible.

questions.question: What does operational memory solve in AI SRE?
options: Cold start of inference pods, a serving-latency problem the lesson does not connect to operational memory
Loss of tribal knowledge when teams turn over — runbooks and post-mortems live in a vector DB that agents retrieve on every incident
Network egress filtering, a security-posture problem the lesson does not connect to operational memory
Token cost attribution, a FinOps problem the lesson does not connect to operational memory
questions.explanation: The lesson frames team turnover as the silent killer of traditional SRE, and operational memory addresses it by storing runbooks and post-mortems in a vector DB that agents retrieve on every new incident, so new engineers inherit the full history.

questions.question: What MIT 2025 result does the lesson cite for pre-incident prediction?
options: Predictions remain unsolved, since the lesson treats pre-incident prediction as not yet technically feasible
10% with no lead time, a figure the lesson does not attach to any prediction study it discusses
89% of outages predicted 10-15 minutes early using logs + GPU temps + API error patterns
100% prediction with 1-second lead, a perfect and instantaneous result the lesson does not claim
questions.explanation: The lesson reports 89%+ lead-time prediction accuracy (logs + GPU temps + API error patterns) as a figure that circulates in vendor blogs and conference talks, and explicitly cautions to treat any specific number as unverified until you re-measure it on your own data.

questions.question: What operational constraint does the lesson stress about predictive detection?
options: Predictions without actuation are just dashboards — the operational question is what action (pre-drain, page, auto-scale) the prediction triggers
Predictions replace runbooks, since the lesson treats prediction as a substitute for documented response steps
Predictions should never be wired to action, since the lesson treats actuation as inherently unsafe
Predictions are always accurate, so the lesson treats the actuation question as unnecessary to answer
questions.explanation: The lesson's reality check is that predictions without actuation are dashboards, not SRE -- the operational question is what specific action (pre-emptive drain, page, auto-scale) a prediction triggers, and that answer is policy-specific.
